chunks.text: Despite its two most common English names, traveller's tree and traveller's palm, Ravenala madagascariensis is not a palm at all — it belongs to its own small family, Strelitziaceae, making it a close relative of the bird-of-paradise flower rather than of true palms, and some older classification schemes grouped it with bananas instead. It is endemic to Madagascar, where mature plants build a sturdy grey trunk topped by a dramatic, flattened fan of thirty to forty-five enormous paddle-shaped leaves held in a single plane, each leaf stalk capable of stretching several metres; the largest-growing wild form, found in the island's eastern highland forests, can reach some 30 metres, dwarfing the roughly 7-metre average typical of cultivated specimens seen in parks and gardens elsewhere in the tropics. Its white flowers, structurally similar to those of its Strelitzia cousins, are pollinated in their native range chiefly by ruffed lemurs, a relationship researchers believe may have coevolved given how precisely the lemur's long muzzle and selective feeding habits match the flower's size and shape; elsewhere in the world, where no lemurs exist, bats and nectar-feeding birds sometimes take over the job instead. The common 'traveller's' name is popularly explained by the rainwater that collects in the cup-like base of each leaf stalk, said to offer thirsty travellers an emergency drink, though in practice this trapped water is just as often fouled by mosquito larvae and debris and is not something to rely on; a second, more mundane explanation offered for the name is that the fan of leaves tends to align on a roughly east-west axis, giving it a rough use as a natural compass.

chunks.source: PROTA (Plant Resources of Tropical Africa) database entry, via plantuse.plantnet.org
chunks.text: This applied-use database fills in the practical, everyday roles the traveller's tree plays across its range, well beyond its fame as an ornamental curiosity. Along Madagascar's east coast, rural households build entire structures from its parts: leaves thatch the roof, split petioles form wall panels, and the bark provides flooring material, while in parts of India introduced plantings are used similarly for stems in house framing, leaves for roofing and packing material, and midribs for hut walls. The seeds, enclosed in a strikingly blue to purple fleshy covering, are edible though starchy and rather bland, and an oil pressed from them is used in local cooking and reputed, though not rigorously confirmed, to have antiseptic properties; sap tapped from the trunk can also be reduced into a crude sugar, and the fibrous pith left over from processing is fed to livestock. Ecologically, the entry records at least four distinct wild growth forms recognised within eastern Madagascar alone, ranging from a rare shade-tolerant understorey form to a vigorously suckering form that is the one most often propagated by growers, and notes the plant can become the dominant colonising species across deforested hill slopes in the 300-to-600-metre elevation band. It also flags two documented pest relationships of agricultural relevance in India: the tree can host the fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, a cause of leaf spot disease in areca nut palm plantations, and its roots are susceptible to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita.
